prose:
Epoch AI demonstrates that a widely available open-weight model can now weaponize the patch gap - the window between a security fix being published and reaching users. In their experiments, GLM 5.3, released by Z.ai in August, took published-but-unshipped Firefox security fixes and turned them into working exploits: a webpage that, when visited, read a file from the visitor's computer and sent it to an attacker with no further interaction. Every Firefox version released between September 17 and October 26 could be compromised using only information available at that version's release, and in each case the model also found and used an unpublished vulnerability alongside the known ones.

The economics are the point. Exploiting the patch gap used to require significant time and expertise, or access to frontier models with advanced cyber capabilities; Epoch's setup deliberately emulates a relatively unsophisticated actor and still succeeds for about $1,000 per Firefox version. The patch gap exists across browsers, phone operating systems and router firmware, so the finding generalizes beyond any one vendor: open-weight models are compressing the skill and cost floor for a class of attacks that was previously out of reach for most actors.
highlights: GLM 5.3, an open-weight model from Z.ai, turns published Firefox fixes into working exploits
Demo: a webpage that reads a file from a visitor's machine and exfiltrates it, no further interaction
Every Firefox release from Sept 17 to Oct 26 compromisable with only release-time information
Model also found and used an unpublished vulnerability in each compromise
Cost: about $1,000 per Firefox version, in a setup mimicking an unsophisticated actor
Patch gap spans browsers, phone OSes and router firmware - the finding generalizes
